Sound familiar?

You spend the whole day bracing for the next one

  • You're parenting an autistic, ADHD or PDA child, and school pick-up, bedtime and getting out of the door all feel like a gamble.
  • You've tried sticker charts, consequences and calm voices, and none of it seems to land.
  • Advice that works for other families seems to make things harder in yours.
  • You're exhausted, and you just want your home to feel safe and calm again.

Here's what you'll learn

Five steps we'll cover in 60 minutes

Why a meltdown isn't bad behaviour

What's happening in your child's nervous system, and why rewards and consequences often don't reach it.

Spotting the build-up early

The quiet signs that come before a meltdown, so you can step in before it peaks.

Why demands land differently

How everyday requests can feel like pressure for some children, and simple low-demand ways to say the same thing.

What to do in the moment

How to stay steady yourself and keep everyone safe when a meltdown is already happening.

Rebuilding calm afterwards

How to reconnect after a hard moment, and set up the next day so there's less to brace for.

Questions

Before you save your seat

Does my child need a diagnosis for this to help?

No. The class is about understanding meltdowns and what's behind them. It's useful whether you have a diagnosis, are on a waiting list, or simply recognise your family in it.

What if I can't make it live?

Your free seat includes the replay, so you can watch once the house is quiet.

Is this therapy or medical advice?

No. It's an educational parenting class. It isn't therapy, diagnosis or medical advice. Please speak to your GP or your child's care team about any health concerns.

Why is it free?

Because the first step should be easy when you're already exhausted. Come along, take what helps, and decide afterwards if you'd like more support.

Educational content, not medical advice.

Live online · FreeSign up

Script 1 · "Not bad behaviour"

Hook (0 to 3s)

"The thing I wish every parent of a neurodivergent child knew about meltdowns."

Body

"A meltdown isn't a child choosing to be difficult. It's a nervous system that's gone past what it can cope with. That's why rewards and consequences so often don't touch it. As a SEN teacher and a mum who's living it, I teach parents a different way: spot the build-up, lower the demands, stay steady in the moment, and reconnect afterwards."

CTA

"I'm running a free live masterclass on the five steps. It's 60 minutes and the replay is included. Tap Sign up to save a seat."

Shot: Laura talking to camera at the kitchen table, warm natural light, mug in hand. No children on camera.

Caption footer: Educational content, not medical advice.

Script 2 · "The school pick-up"

Hook (0 to 3s)

"For so many families, the hardest part of the day starts at 3:15."

Body

"A child holds it together all day at school, then it all comes out at the car door. Parents tell me they spend the drive home bracing for it. There are early signs that come before a meltdown, and small changes to the first hour home that can make it feel very different."

CTA

"I'll walk through them in my free Calm Home Masterclass. Live, 60 minutes. Tap Sign up."

Shot: Laura in the car (parked) or by the front door, talking to camera. Text on screen: "3:15pm". No children on camera.

Caption footer: Educational content, not medical advice.

Script 3 · "Same words, less pressure"

Hook (0 to 3s)

"Here's one sentence parents swap out that changes how the morning goes."

Body

"For some children, a direct instruction like 'put your shoes on' feels like pressure, even when it's said kindly. Swapping it for something like 'I wonder where the shoes are hiding' asks for the same thing with less demand. That's step three of the five I teach."

CTA

"Get all five in my free live masterclass. Replay included. Tap Sign up below."

Shot: Laura holding up two cards ("Put your shoes on" / "I wonder where the shoes are hiding"), on-screen text for each.

Caption footer: Educational content, not medical advice.
